Chapter 9: The Role of Technology and the Future of Work
As our world keeps changing, the challenges facing any vision of a just society change too. And right now, technology is at the heart of it all, reshaping the way we live and work at a pace that can feel pretty overwhelming. The author approaches this with both urgency and hope.
Picture this: you walk into a warehouse, and instead of people moving boxes, you see robots gliding around, lifting and sorting, while computers track every single item. For some folks, it’s a stunning example of efficiency. But for others, it’s a source of real anxiety. Workers worry about their jobs disappearing, while managers scramble to keep up with new pressures and demands. The old rules? They just don’t seem to fit anymore.
Most of us don’t even realize how much technology is shaping our daily lives. Algorithms quietly decide what news pops up on our screens, what jobs show up in our feeds—even who we might meet. In some places, tech has made life simpler and more connected. But in others, it’s widened the gap, leaving people feeling even more isolated and left behind.
So, what does the new socialism need to do in this world? It’s not enough to just promise more jobs or better wages. The real challenge is giving people true control over technology—instead of letting technology control them. That means investing in education and supporting lifelong learning, so everyone can keep up and make the most of the tools out there.
Here’s a story that brings this to life. There was a group of gig workers who’d had enough of low pay and unpredictable hours. So, they came together and built their own cooperative platform. They created an app, set fair rates, and shared the profits. It wasn’t all smooth sailing—there were tech headaches and debates over the best way forward—but, in the end, they found something powerful: real empowerment and a sense of solidarity.
What became clear is that technology isn’t fate. The choices we make—about who owns the tools, how they’re designed, and how they’re regulated—those choices shape our future. The author makes a strong case: a just society has to make sure technology serves the common good, not just private profit.
So, what’s the big takeaway here? The future of work isn’t just about machines or markets. It’s about dignity, agency, and the real chance to build a better life. If the new socialism wants to meet this moment, it has to be bold enough to imagine new possibilities—and humble enough to keep learning as we go.
